title: HarperCollins Is Launching Kazé in the U.S., and Manga Publishing Just Got a New Heavyweight
description: HarperCollins is launching a dedicated U.S. manga imprint under the Kazé name, with seven initial licenses to be revealed later in 2026 and books spanning children through adult readers.
dek: This is bigger than a seven-title license drop. One of the world's largest trade publishers is turning a revived European manga brand into a dedicated U.S. imprint.

hero.alt: AniManga Updates with Old Man Otaku

blocks.html: The English-language manga market is getting another serious publishing player. HarperCollins has announced a new U.S. manga imprint called Kazé, with an initial lineup of seven licenses scheduled to be revealed later in 2026. The imprint is being built to publish across age categories, from children's titles through manga for adult readers.

That makes this more important than a routine license announcement. HarperCollins is not simply acquiring a handful of manga. It is establishing a dedicated U.S. manga identity inside one of the largest trade-publishing operations in the world.
Kazé Is New to the U.S. Plan, but the Name Has History

Kazé is not a brand HarperCollins invented this week. The French company dates to 1994 and became part of VIZ Media Europe in 2009. It later operated within Crunchyroll's European business, and the Kazé publishing name was replaced by Crunchyroll branding in 2022.

The corporate path changed again in 2025 when HarperCollins acquired Crunchyroll's manga-publishing operations in France and Germany. HarperCollins subsequently revived the historic KAZÉ name for those businesses, with the restored branding taking effect for new European releases beginning in April 2026. The newly announced American imprint therefore looks less like a random startup label and more like the next geographic expansion of a manga operation HarperCollins has already been rebuilding.
The First Seven Licenses Are Still Under Wraps

ICv2 reports that Kazé's first U.S. lineup will consist of seven titles, all scheduled to be announced later in 2026. The actual series have not been revealed yet, so any list circulating before HarperCollins makes those announcements should be treated as speculation.

What has been confirmed is the breadth of the imprint's intended readership. Kazé will publish manga for multiple age groups, including children and adults. That is an important strategic clue: HarperCollins does not appear to be positioning Kazé as a narrow shonen-only label or a single-demographic experiment.
HarperCollins Was Already Publishing Manga

The announcement also needs one correction to the easy headline. HarperCollins is not entering manga from absolute zero. It already publishes manga, including mamakari's Plus-Sized Misadventures in Love!, and HarperAlley has published graphic novels marketed within the manga category. ICv2 specifically notes that Plus-Sized Misadventures in Love! bears Kazé branding.

The meaningful change is dedication and scale. A named U.S. imprint gives manga its own publishing identity, editorial lane and brand-building opportunity rather than leaving individual manga titles dispersed across a broader trade list.
Why HarperCollins Changes the Competitive Picture

The North American manga shelf is already crowded with experienced specialists and major publishing groups. VIZ Media, Kodansha, Yen Press, Seven Seas and others have built recognizable catalogs, licensing relationships and reader communities over years. HarperCollins does not erase those advantages by putting a new logo on seven books.

What HarperCollins brings is mainstream publishing infrastructure. Its U.S. trade operation sits inside a global publisher with deep relationships across bookstores, online retail, libraries, schools, marketing and distribution. That can matter enormously when the challenge is not merely licensing a manga, but putting it in front of readers who may never visit an anime convention or specialty comic shop.

The move also arrives while other publishers continue expanding manga programs. Kodansha used Anime Expo and Comic-Con 2026 to announce additional North American print licenses, while Seven Seas continues adding manga, light novels, manhwa and other Asian-origin publishing categories. Kazé is entering an active market, not an empty one.
The European Acquisition Explains the Timing

The timing makes more sense when viewed through HarperCollins' European moves. After acquiring Crunchyroll's French and German manga publishing operations in 2025, HarperCollins gained teams, backlists, production knowledge and an established manga brand with decades of recognition in parts of Europe. The restored Kazé operation describes itself as focused specifically on manga publishing, while Crunchyroll retained streaming, home-entertainment and merchandise businesses.

In other words, HarperCollins did not simply wake up and decide manga looked fashionable. It bought publishing infrastructure, revived a known manga label and is now preparing to extend that identity into the United States.
What We Still Don't Know

The identities of the first seven U.S. licenses
The first U.S. publication dates
Which Japanese publishers Kazé's initial U.S. licenses will come from
Whether Kazé will emphasize print, digital or simultaneous formats
Its exact editorial leadership and staffing for the U.S. list
How aggressively HarperCollins plans to scale beyond the first seven titles
Those unanswered questions will determine whether Kazé becomes a modest specialist list or a major new force. The announcement establishes intent. The first licenses will reveal strategy.
The Old Man Otaku Take

The most interesting part of this announcement is not the number seven. Seven licenses can be a launch slate. Seven licenses can also disappear into a bookstore catalog without changing much of anything.

The important part is the name above them: HarperCollins. A publisher with that kind of retail and distribution reach deciding that manga deserves a dedicated American imprint is another sign that English-language manga is being treated as a durable publishing category rather than a temporary boom.

Kazé now has to prove it can become more than corporate muscle wearing a manga jacket. The first seven titles need an identity. They need readers to understand why Kazé exists when the market already has established publishers competing for attention every week.

RogueVerse takeaway: HarperCollins already had manga on its shelves. Kazé turns that activity into a dedicated U.S. publishing strategy, backed by a revived European manga brand and the infrastructure of a global trade-publishing giant. Watch the first seven licenses. They will tell us whether this is a new shelf label or the beginning of a real market challenger.
